title: Pancreatic Cancer or Acidity? Warning Signs, Blood Tests and the Diagnostic Pathway
description: How to distinguish common indigestion from symptoms that warrant pancreatic evaluation: back pain, weight loss, jaundice, new diabetes, CA 19-9 limits, CT and EUS.

faq.question: Can acidity be an early sign of pancreatic cancer?
faq.answer: Indigestion can occur in people with pancreatic cancer, but acidity is very common and usually has other causes. Persistent or changing symptoms with weight loss, jaundice or back pain need assessment.

faq.question: Can pancreatic cancer cause back pain without jaundice?
faq.answer: Yes. Some patients have upper-abdominal or back pain without jaundice; this is especially possible when the bile duct is not obstructed.

faq.question: Does a normal CA 19-9 rule out pancreatic cancer?
faq.answer: No. CA 19-9 is neither a screening nor a rule-out test. Some patients with pancreatic cancer have normal CA 19-9.

faq.question: Can amylase and lipase identify pancreatic cancer?
faq.answer: No. They are used mainly when pancreatitis is suspected and cannot diagnose or exclude pancreatic malignancy.

faq.question: Which scan is best when cancer is suspected?
faq.answer: A contrast-enhanced pancreas-protocol multiphasic CT is a central imaging test; MRI/MRCP or EUS may be added based on clinical findings.

faq.question: Should all people with diabetes have CA 19-9 testing?
faq.answer: No. Diabetes is common. The combination of new diabetes with unexplained weight loss or other red flags warrants clinical risk assessment, not automatic CA 19-9 screening.

faq.question: Is pancreatic cancer curable?
faq.answer: Some early, operable cases may be treated with curative intent using surgery and systemic treatment. Outcomes depend on stage, tumour biology and specialist assessment.

faq.question: Can blood tests find bile duct obstruction?
faq.answer: Liver biochemistry can suggest cholestasis but imaging is required to identify the cause and location.

faq.question: Where can I get a CA 19-9 test in Bengaluru?
faq.answer: QXL Diagnostics lists CA 19-9 in its oncology and gastroenterology services. It should be ordered and interpreted with appropriate specialist advice.

faq.question: When is jaundice an emergency?
faq.answer: Yellow eyes with fever, chills, abdominal pain, confusion or severe illness needs emergency care because bile-duct infection can become life threatening.

title: Early Warning Signs of Pancreatic Cancer: Symptoms, Signs and When to Seek Care
description: Understand 15 possible pancreatic cancer symptoms, red-flag combinations, common mimics and when to seek urgent imaging.

faq.question: What is the most common first symptom?
faq.answer: There is no single reliable first symptom. Many patients have vague pain, weight loss or no early symptoms.

faq.question: Can pancreatic cancer occur without jaundice?
faq.answer: Yes. Jaundice depends partly on whether a tumour obstructs bile drainage.

faq.question: Does back pain always mean pancreatic cancer?
faq.answer: No. Musculoskeletal pain is much more common; persistent back pain with weight loss or abdominal symptoms warrants clinical assessment.

title: CA 19-9 Test for Pancreatic Cancer: Meaning, False Positives and When to Order
description: What CA 19-9 measures, why a high or normal result cannot diagnose pancreatic cancer, Lewis antigen limitations and monitoring uses.

faq.question: What is the normal CA 19-9 range?
faq.answer: Use the reference interval printed by the performing laboratory for its assay; there is no single result that confirms or excludes pancreatic cancer.

faq.question: Can jaundice raise CA 19-9?
faq.answer: Yes. Bile-duct obstruction and related inflammation can cause elevations independent of cancer.

faq.question: Is CA 19-9 a cancer screening test?
faq.answer: No. It is not recommended as a screening test in average-risk people without symptoms.

title: Pancreatic Cancer Blood Tests vs CT, MRI, EUS and Biopsy: Diagnostic Guide
description: Learn what LFT, CBC, glucose, amylase, lipase, CA 19-9, CT, MRI/MRCP, EUS and biopsy can and cannot show.

faq.question: Can a normal LFT exclude pancreatic cancer?
faq.answer: No. A pancreatic tumour may exist without bile-duct obstruction.

faq.question: Is ultrasound enough to rule out pancreatic cancer?
faq.answer: Not when clinical suspicion remains high; CT, MRI/MRCP or EUS may be required.

faq.question: Does everyone need a biopsy before surgery?
faq.answer: Not always. The specialist MDT decides based on imaging, resectability and treatment plan.

title: New-Onset Diabetes and Weight Loss: When Should the Pancreas Be Evaluated?
description: How new or worsening diabetes with unexplained weight loss can prompt a physician to consider pancreatic disease without indiscriminate CA 19-9 testing.

faq.question: Does new diabetes mean pancreatic cancer?
faq.answer: No. The great majority of new diabetes cases are not pancreatic cancer.

faq.question: Is HbA1c a pancreatic cancer test?
faq.answer: No. It measures average blood glucose exposure and cannot identify tumour cause.

faq.question: Should new diabetes with weight loss prompt imaging?
faq.answer: A clinician should assess age, weight change and other red flags and may request timely pancreatic imaging.

faq.question: Can gallstones cause jaundice and pale stools?
faq.answer: Yes, gallstones can obstruct the bile duct and produce the same pattern.

faq.question: Can pancreatic cancer cause painless jaundice?
faq.answer: Yes; painless jaundice is one possible presentation, but other causes exist.

faq.question: Will bilirubin tell whether obstruction is cancer?
faq.answer: No. Blood tests indicate a physiological pattern; imaging and specialist evaluation identify the cause.

title: Greasy Floating Stool and Pancreatic Insufficiency: When Is Faecal Elastase Useful?
description: Greasy stools, weight loss and pancreatic exocrine insufficiency: how stool elastase fits into the clinical workup and why it is not a cancer test.

faq.question: Is floating stool always pancreatic disease?
faq.answer: No. Stool can float for several benign reasons. Greasy, frequent stool with weight loss deserves clinical assessment.

faq.question: Does low faecal elastase mean cancer?
faq.answer: No. It suggests possible exocrine insufficiency but does not identify the cause.

faq.question: Can watery stool affect faecal elastase?
faq.answer: Yes. Excess water can dilute the sample and produce a falsely low measurement.

title: Family History of Pancreatic Cancer: Genetic Risk and Who Needs Surveillance
description: Why average-risk people do not need pancreatic cancer blood-test screening and how selected high-risk families may qualify for MRI/EUS surveillance.

faq.question: Can CA 19-9 screen people with family history?
faq.answer: Not reliably. Selected high-risk people need specialist risk assessment and an imaging surveillance pathway.

faq.question: Does one affected relative always mean surveillance?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Gene status, number and relationship of affected relatives and age at diagnosis affect eligibility.

faq.question: Should relatives undergo genetic counselling?
faq.answer: Genetic counselling is useful when family history or known inherited variants suggest a hereditary syndrome.

title: Gastritis, GERD or Pancreatic Pain? A Clinical Symptom Comparison
description: Compare reflux, H. pylori gastritis, gallstones, pancreatitis and pancreatic red flags using symptom pattern and appropriate investigations.

faq.question: Does pancreatic pain always radiate to the back?
faq.answer: No. Back radiation may occur but is not required and is not specific for cancer.

faq.question: Can H. pylori cause indigestion?
faq.answer: Yes. It can be associated with gastritis and ulcers; testing should follow a clinician-selected dyspepsia pathway.

faq.question: Should persistent acidity always trigger CA 19-9?
faq.answer: No. CA 19-9 is not suitable as a routine dyspepsia screening test.
